speechtext:
MEASURETO enact
The House resumed from Thursday, February 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-105, an Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We should now be in the question and comment period of the speech of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) on Bill C-105. If there are no questions or comments, we will proceed with debate.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that Bill C-105, with respect to rail safety, is a very important Bill. Any Member of Parliament from Winnipeg should have a major interest in all questions of rail safety. The maintenance shops for both railways which employ thousands of railway workers is in Winnipeg. It is a city which is the turn-around point for most traffic, passenger and freight, therefore gives employment to a great many workers who actually move the trains.
When one looks at the record of this industry with respect to safety and sees the number of collisions and derailments that have taken place in recent years, one cannot help but feel that it is not only important that we discuss it thoroughly but that a Bill of this nature should have been brought forth years ago.
I have some figures obtained from the Department of Transport and they are, to say the least, shocking. In the last five years, from 1983 to 1987, there were 1,318 derailments across the country. There were 423 collisions and 3,437 crossing accidents which resulted in the death of 361 people. We are talking about a very serious situation, a situation which should have been dealt with a long time ago.
What are some of the reasons we have had so many accidents which have led to well over 300 fatalities? My colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin),
talked about one of the problems yesterday, that is, the thousands of level crossings across Canada. I do not believe there is another industrialized country in the world which has permitted so many railway level crossings to continue to exist. It is true that because of our relatively small population and because of the large area which Canada covers, there is no way in which we could get rid of level crossings as rapidly and effectively as they have in European countries.
The process has also been slowed down to a snail's pace because of the necessity for local communities to participate financially in doing away with level crossings. In my own part of Winnipeg alone where one level crossing was done away with, and another was projected, we were looking at expenditures of more than $10 million in each case, which required the city and the province to participate at a time when their financial ability to pay part of the cost is, to say the least, very difficult.
There is another reason for the number of derailments and accidents, that is, the cut-back and the reductions of the railways in their expenditures for maintenance of equipment and of trackage. This is a long-standing fact which has been brought to the attention of Governments, the former Liberal Government and the present Conservative Government, and by unions such as the Brotherhood of Maintenance and Way Employees whose members work on improving, maintaining or repairing tracks. Other unions such as the one to which the carmen belong have also complained about the continued use of rail cars and freight trains which have defects and need repairing.
The Government's decision to deregulate railway transportation will mean that the railway companies will find it much more difficult to compete not only between themselves but with alternative methods of transportation such as trucks and ships. If railway companies like any other companies have to compete and worry about whether they can continue to keep the kind and volume of traffic they have served in the past or to obtain more traffic, then one of the ways that they will try to compete is by cutting back on the maintenance of their equipment and their tracks. What we will see are more accidents, more collisions, more derailments and, I am sorry to say, more deaths as a result of these cut-backs. The morale of railway workers has gone down, down, down in my City of Winnipeg. I am sure that in other cities it has also gone down. It was not unusual to see working for the railways either in the running trades or in the maintenance shops second and third generation workers whose fathers and grandfathers worked for

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
the same railway. The feeling of loyalty, the feeling that the railway was a good place to work is much less now than it once was. It will decrease more in the future. The reasons for this are very simple.
When I became a Member of Parliament the railway unions negotiated for over 200,000 members. Today, they negotiate for fewer than 75,000 members. In the relentless determination of the railways to be more efficient, which really means more profitable, they have cut employment to the bone. Thus people working for the railways now are not likely to advise their sons or daughters that they should think about working for the railways. Rather, they will be advising their children to look elsewhere for work.
Before the election the Government talked and still talks about its determination, its desire to consult with people who are affected concerning a certain question in any area in which the Government wants to make progress or to change the way that things are done. In the legislation that is before us the Government wants the companies to have the right to be able to perform random checks of their employees to protect the railways and the public against those who have been drinking or using drugs. 1 can understand the concern of the Government. I can understand the concern of the railways and their unions. I can understand the concern of the public. There have been accidents in which there seems to be evidence that some employees running the train had been using alcohol or drugs that cannot be excused.
Surely the way for a Government which believes in consultation and for railway companies which have more than 50 years of collective bargaining with their employees behind them to deal with the problem is not in a ham-fisted and tough way saying, "We are going to amend the legislation so we can decide unilaterally and in a random way that employees will be tested for drug or alcohol use". Surely, the way to cut back on the dangers and the problems which can arise, which do arise and which will arise if railway employees use drugs or alcohol while working is for railway management to sit down with the leaders of the unions representing their workers and together work out a system of education. In this way the use of alcohol and drugs which takes place among a small percentage of railway workers, as it does among a small percentage of any group of Canadians wherever they work, can be dealt with.
The former Liberal Government was, as is the present Government, driven by the determination that the railways have to become cost efficient and that their deficits have to be reduced or eliminated. The concern about employees, whether it be with respect to their number or anything else, has become a small factor, if it is a factor at all, for the management of the two national railway companies.
This legislation is deficient in many ways. Its objectives may sound right, but it will not succeed.
I wish to refer to another aspect of this legislation which was referred to by my friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). It is the question of stress and how it
affects rail safety and the accidents which occur on railways. I refer Hon. Members to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail of yesterday entitled: "Stress rides the rails". It is an article written by Professor Brian Tucker who teaches at the University of Saskatchewan's College of Commerce. He states in the article:
Three train accidents in as many days last month claimed four lives, injured 35 and caused millions of dollars in damage. The latest episodes in the continuing saga of death and destruction on our railways, they point a spotlight on stress research. A year ago, a locomotive engineer came to see me to talk about the stress he was experiencing from his job. He talked about the trauma trainmen undergo when a car is hit at a crossing.
Earlier I referred to the number of crossing accidents that we have had. There have been almost 3,500 in the last five years.
The article further states:
He described the sickening feeling when an engineer realizes there is no way he can stop thousands of tons of locomotive in time.
That is one experience. There are dozens, if not hundreds, of railway employees who have been involved in an accident. After there has been an accident, a collision, or a derailment, an inquiry is held between the railways and the Department of Transport to find out what happened and who was responsible. In many cases, they come to the conclusion that the engineer, the trainman, and the conductor were not responsible, the accident resulted from factors beyond their control, and they were absolved. But just because they are absolved does not mean that they can quickly forget about it. Not in the railways, but in many companies there are personnel departments with people who are trained, for example, including social workers, psychologists, or psychiatrists on a consulting basis, or social workers who can work with the employees and help them overcome the trauma and the tremendous feeling of guilt that they must have, even when they have been absolved of responsibility.
The railways have been loath to do that, either because they do not understand the importance, or possibly because it would just be another cost at a time when they are being pressed to reduce the cost, and become more efficient, which means cutting back on the financial burdens. In the article, Professor Tucker further states:
Handling stress is a vital part of a manager's job. Managers can and must design jobs and working conditions to ease stress levels .. . When will CP. CN and Via take stress seriously? When will they (and other employers who provide extremely stressful working conditions) realize that proper stress management can prevent disasters?
Professor Tucker asks some very important questions. If we look at the record, the answers are that up until now the railways have been, to say the least, remiss in following the type of procedures and the type of suggestions that Professor Tucker has made in this article. Given the pressure on the railways to become more financially efficient, which means to save money, I suggest that the railways will not voluntarily
February 5, 1988

follow the advice of Professor Tucker, and similar advice given to them many times by the railway union.
Rather than simply passing this Bill and including in it the right of companies or the Department to test employees on a random basis, the Department and the Government ought to be saying to the railways that it is time they started to deal with these very serious problems in a realistic manner. It is time to sit down with the employees, through their unions, and start to develop programs which will encourage workers to avoid the use of drugs and alcohol when they are on their way to work.
In that way, on a year to year steady basis, we will begin to see a reduction-which we have not so far seen-in the number of train derailments, train collisions, railway crossing accidents, and certainly a reduction in the number of deaths which result from rail accidents.
In my Province of Manitoba we have had a number of derailments. There was one in the centre of the city in the CPR yards where trains are moving and switching. In that derailment freight cars containing highly toxic chemicals left the track. In Winnipeg there could have been a situation as critical and dangerous to hundreds of people as the derailment in Mississauga a few years ago.
Those derailments could be avoided, or certainly the numbers could be minimized, if the railways were required to take the type of precautions that they have been urged to do, the identification of cars carrying dangerous chemicals, and much better planning of movement of freight which has potentially dangerous chemicals or other products on board. The railways have to do a much better job. They will not do a much better job unless the Government and the Department of Transport sit down with the railway management and with the unions and work out a program which will lead to the thinking and planning that will decrease, if not completely eliminate, the accidents and the situations that we have seen happen much too frequently in recent years.
While we are not going to oppose this Bill, we certainly think that there is a great deal that should be in the Bill which is not there.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The Hon. Member has emphasized at considerable length the reduction of persons employed by the railways over a period of time, and I would suggest that this is in direct relation to the reduction in the number of miles travelled by the railways, and the accidents have been related accordingly. One of the greatest railway disasters which hit western Canada was the one that happened in Alberta. As a result of that accident, an inquiry took place conducted by the Hon. Mr. Justice Foisy. In his report Mr. Justice Foisy pointed out that no fault could be laid regarding the integrity of the system, the operation of the mechanics, or whatever signal system was in place. As the Hon. Member knows, it means that in this instance that
Railway Safety Act
disaster took place by reason of human fault. The Hon. Member, and all of us, are very concerned with the safety of railways and a reduction in the number of accidents. Is it fair to say, if human fault is one of the major causes of rail derailments or head-on collisions, that we should work together to find ways and means of reducing, not excusing, the number of incidents which take place?
The Hon. Member indicated that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) might be inclined to impose compulsory, random testing for alcohol or drug abuse. I remind the Hon. Member that a committee was formed, comprised of union people, management personnel, and people involved in safety. That committee reached a conclusion and reported.
1 will refer to some of its findings. For example, 7 per cent of those surveyed were aware of workers drinking alcoholic beverages during shifts, 4 per cent were aware of drugs on the job, 52 per cent said that alcohol used by employees had compromised job safety at some time or other during the course of a run, and 48 per cent said that mandatory drug testing of railway personnel was desirable.
The Minister has not taken that position. He said that we must provide for a position where testing for alcohol and drugs takes place to determine what is the cause of an accident. If it is drug or alcohol, and the number of events justifies such course of action at a later date, then the Minister would be prepared to review and make a recommendation accordingly, in the interest of safety. Is that not a fair conclusion to take, in the interest of safety?

Mr. Speaker, nothing I said is contradictory or opposed to what the Hon. Member has just said. The accident at Hinton and many other accidents were caused entirely or in part by human failure, and part of human failure is the use of drugs or alcohol by railway employees.
Why should we be surprised about that? A huge majority of automobile accidents, particularly those which lead to the death of passengers, occurs because one or the other of the drivers of the cars was under the influence of liquor or drugs. The same is true when it comes to railway accidents. I tried to say that when I spoke earlier.
The way to deal with that, if we really want results, is not by the Minister calling for random or mandatory tests. It is not for the railways to implement unilaterally what they believe to be the best educational program. Because of the very marked reduction in the number of railway employees, because of the worry of railway employees that they may not have a job a year or two or five from now, and because of many other reasons, morale among railway workers is very low. Therefore, any unilateral proposal by the companies is looked on with a great deal of suspicion by the employees and by their unions.
I say again to the Hon. Member who has asked the question that if we want to succeed, we need co-operation, discussion,

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
and development of programs. This must be done co-operatively among the companies and their management, the workers and their unions, and the Government-the Department of Transport and hopefully the Department of Health and Welfare. If we develop those kinds of educational information programs, I believe that-and I have had a good deal of experience working with unions in many ways-they would be accepted by the vast majority of workers. There would be real reason to believe that those kinds of programs would be successful. If we implemented such programs, we would begin to see a marked reduction over a period of years in the kinds of accidents which have taken place and which all of us regret.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North. I do not think any one of us can really get into a debate on why the morale of the railway workers is low. One reason might be is that they have failed to accept reality.
The position taken by the Hon. Member is such that he does not want any unilateral action to be taken by railway management. If that is the case, I suggest to him that the unions are free to take whatever attitude and action they want to take now to improve morale and safety of the railways. It is just as much in their interest as it is in that of management.
What action has the union taken from the point of view of improving morale, accepting the reality of the situation that exists in the industry today, and ensuring that the number of derailments and other incidents are reduced?
I emphasize the hard premise the Hon. Member comes down on that no unilateral action may be taken by railway management. The union members on the task force to which I referred a moment ago were prepared to recommend a harder line that the one taken by the Minister. They did not adopt that, nor has the Minister of Transport. He is prepared to work out a process of safety regulation in conjunction with the unions rather than take the recommendation which was put forward. That is the approach the Minister has taken in respect of safety in the railway transportation segment in years to come. I hope that it works, and I hope that with the cooperation of the Hon. Member we will get it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the Hon. Member would suggest, as he did a moment ago, or even believe or think that railway workers and their unions are not prepared to face reality. They have had to live with the reality that in the period of less than 25 years the number of railway employees for whom the unions bargain has been reduced from well over 200,000 to under 75,000. They have had to live with that reality, and they have had to accept it.
I point out to the Hon. Member that the main point of contention between the striking group of railway workers whom we legislated back to work last August and the companies was the demand for improvement of the job security system. The main issue of contention of the shopcraft workers who are just waiting to go on strike and with whom the
railways have stopped negotiating is the whole question of job security. They have faced reality.
Let me say just one more thing. I have not said for a moment that I am opposed to any kind of unilateral program initiated by the companies or by the Government. What I have said is that if any proposals, suggestions or programs that are designed to help cut back the number of railway accidents, crossing accidents and derailments are to work, they will work much better if they are planned and implemented through consultation, discussion and co-operation between the Government, the Departments responsible, the railway management and the workers on the job through their unions. Without that kind of co-operation, unfortunately in my belief, tragically the programs will fail.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words on Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. We have seen enough derailments and accidents on rail lines in the last several years. Legislation in this regard is desperately needed. This Bill may be a starting point, but our side sees a lot of weaknesses in the Bill and we want to see it strengthened if it is to pass in the House after going to committee. When the Bill does go to committee, we hope the Government will be open and prepared to deal with the issues and the amendments needed to make the legislation effective. I say that because when drafters of a Bill put it together they often overlook weaknesses, and sometimes do not even deal with all of the existing legislation needing amendment.
A few weeks ago, we had Bill C-92 before the Agriculture Committee which had to do with the use of producer cars. That legislation provided for a refund of services by farmers in western Canada who use producer railway cars. These included carrying costs and interest charges et cetera. As the witnesses give their testimony before the committee it became apparent that the Bill did not really deal with all aspects. There was an extra cost in the maintenance of country elevator delivery points by using individual producer cars. This cost was being charged by the railroads to the general cost of transporting grain in western Canada. We had the situation where we had an inadequate Bill because it did not cover transportation costs. It only covered those costs are refundable through the Canadian Wheat Board.
Unfortunately, government Members on the committee refused to agree to spend the extra time to have all that information put before the committee. The same thing will apply to this legislation. Obviously we perceive many weaknesses. If we can deal with those weaknesses without the hammer of the Government's majority coming down, it will make for a better situation in dealing with legislation as important as public safety. Clearly we need improvement in the legislation.
We saw the Hinton train disaster in 1986 when 23 people were killed. Accidents have occurred in my own constituency
February 5, 1988

with fatal results. Canada is rapidly moving to more and more travel by car and truck. Level crossings are dangerous and we have to deal with the question of the transportation of pesticides.
Deregulation of the railroad inevitably brings on more problems and threatens the safety of rail lines. We see deregulation having tremendous impacts in various parts of the country. The Globe and Mail carried a story yesterday in which the senior Vice-President, Mr. D. L. Fletcher of CNR, said that CN must move ahead rapidly to cut back on the number of employees because a general election might happen later this year. Surely that kind of secret memorandum where the political game is being played without thought of the workers and of their safety is a serious matter.
There is so much secrecy. We read reports and documents that the rail line from Espanola to Sault Ste. Marie in northern Ontario may ultimately be shut down because of deregulation because the volume of traffic carried over the line is something less than 400,000 tonnes a year. Yet when you go to the CPR to get a clear statement of its intentions, you never get an answer in any way, shape or form. This kind of secrecy does not give me much confidence that we will get any information from them on matters of safety.
The whole question of deregulation of the railroad system in this country is designed to make greater use of the American railway lines. It will allow shippers to go to the railway companies requiring them to provide a rate to move produce and lumber, whatever it is, down to the American lines to be moved across the United States. In the trade deal that we recently signed between Canada and the United States, the Government gave away one of the major economic benefits to western Canada by indicating that the Crow benefit, which amounts to some $700 million a year to western grain producers, is, in fact, a subsidy and will no longer be provided to shippers of grain and oil seed to the Pacific northwest.
So we have a situation where the Government in its trade negotiations with the United States is going to the GATT negotiations saying yes, this is a subsidy so it will ultimately be removed. The Government has stated that its policy is to be "a me too policy" to the United States in trade negotiations of the Uruguay round at the GATT. That whole movement of deregulation we see as being in conflict. The responsibility for safety is given to the Minister rather than to the CTC. The Minister is also implementing deregulation which is designed to put more pressure on rail employees to create a more competitive rail system with less regulation and less safety.
Those are some of the concerns we have with this legislation. When we are deregulating and giving over the responsibility for safety to the rail companies, we must also look at how good these large, centralized companies are as corporate citizens. Let us look at the way these companies maintain their buildings and properties in many communities along the north
Railway Safety Act
shore of Lake Huron, those communities from Sudbury to Sault Ste Marie. They certainly do not inspire much confidence. They are usually the worst looking buildings, the worst kept properties and on the worst lands. We just hope that this legislation, when amended, will have enough teeth to provide that the railway companies will not be so bad at keeping the safety of workers as a paramount consideration.
We know how the railway companies have acted in communities like the Garden River Indian Band. Negotiations have been going on for the past seven or eight years over lands which were given to the CPR to build a railway 75 or 100 years ago. The CPR refuses to return those lands which contain rich gravel deposits which could be extremely useful in the economic development of the band. The company refused to negotiate, even after an important legal decision in British Columbia. The company is saying that if the Garden River Indian Band wants the lands returned to it, then let it sue the company. That is just great, but the Garden River Band does not have the funds to carry on a long legal battle.
The corporate citizenship of this company is drawn into question. Can this company which has received tens of millions of dollars of benefits from the Government of Canada, including the railway right-of-way through the land of the Garden River Band, be trusted to be concerned with safety when it shows such incredibly bad corporate citizenship by holding up the development of a major new four-lane highway which would benefit not only the Garden River Band but the general public and the safety of the highways? That whole development has been stalled for several years because of the reluctance of the CPR to give any consideration to the Garden River Band which gave up, through an expropriation by the federal Government, a great deal of land 75 or 100 years ago.
This legislation is of great concern to our caucus as well because of Clause 41 which provides for fines and penalties. A single individual railway worker can be meted out a penalty of $10,000. That seems to be pretty severe and could work an incredible hardship on an individual railway worker, perhaps causing him to pay out his life savings. At the same time, the corporate fine for the railway company, whether it is CN or CP or one of the other billion-dollar corporations, is $50,000 maximum. That is a pittance for a large railway company which might find it more convenient to pay the fine occasionally rather than carry out important safety measures in the operation of the railway, the operation of level crossings or the installation of new equipment which would make the railway safer.
We are concerned about the level of fines and penalties provided by Clause 41 of this legislation. We are also concerned with the composition of the railway safety committees provided for in Clause 44. The clause provides for a committee of a maximum of 11 persons. That may be adequate, but it may not. Canada is a large country. There are 10 provinces and two territories. The size of the committee may not be adequate.

February 5, 1988
We are also concerned with the structure of the committee. The clause provides for only one representative of labour. In practically every train accident where there is a loss of life, labour is almost invariably involved in that loss of life. There is one representative of labour, and labour almost invariably lose lives in major train accidents, but there are six representatives of the railway companies and the railway business. It seems rather uneven. Surely the input from labour is more important than that.
There are two major railway companies and many other smaller railway companies like Algoma Central Railway which runs through my constituency. We will end up having no representation from most of the other railway companies and almost no representation from labour. Of course, four representatives are to be appointed by the Minister. We can imagine what those appointments will be like. We need only read Claire Hoy's book to learn about the whole approach to patronage. Surely this legislation is too important to be concerned with patronage in those Ministerial appointments.
There is no provision for representation from municipalities and cities on the committees. There should be provision for representation on that side as well.
I notice that you are signalling me that Question Period is about to begin, Mr. Speaker. Those are some of the concerns we in this caucus have with Bill C-105 which is before the House today.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), who signed an agreement this week with his American counterpart, under which our two countries will be able to consolidate further their measures against drug trafficking. The consequences of drug use and drug trafficking are a matter of grave concern for the Government and the people of Canada.
To help deal with this problem, the federal Government decided to take the offensive last May by launching its national anti-drug strategy. Tuesday in Washington, the Solicitor General concluded this important agreement with the United States to follow through on the commitment he made in May. The agreement will vastly improve the pooling of
information on drug trafficking, thanks to the work of RCMP officers posted in three American cities.
Mr. Speaker, both countries agree that as a problem that is not only national but also international, drug trafficking must be attacked on all fronts. That is why Canada is placing such emphasis on this agreement and why we have every reason to applaud the Solicitor General's initiative.

subsubtopic: PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY-FORMATION OF BACK BENCH COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the media recently reported that some two dozen male Conservative Members of Parliament formed a very private, indeed secret club, called the BBC, or the Back Bench Committee. Some non-Members call this BBC the Braindead Brontosaurus Committee. Some of us who are more polite call it the Backward Blue Committee. It may turn out to be known as the Blather Bag Committee or, worse, the Brain Baffling Committee. One thing for sure, BBC does not stand for bilingualism and biculturalism.
These prehistoric remnants, these models of antediluvian thought, have lost the first round. We are going to start debating Bill C-72 on Monday. We will debate it thoroughly and I hope they all stand up and tell us what they think about it because we are very interested. They have lost the first battle but they have not lost the war. Let us keep fighting, gentlemen. Get up and tell us what you believe and what you think should be changed in the law. But, for God's sake, let us think of Canada.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF NEW DIRECTOR GENERAL-POSITION OF HULL MAYOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to deplore the statements of Hull Mayor Michel Legere concerning the vacancy in the position of Director General of the National Arts Centre. Mr. Legere, a former, and perhaps future, NDP candidate in this city, is an ex officio member of the board of trustees of the NAC. In that capacity he has insisted that the new Director General be not just bilingual but a Francophone.
February 5, 1988

Most Canadians, and certainly this Member of Parliament, would agree that it is highly desirable that most chief executives of national cultural institutions be able to function in both official languages. To insist, however, that a particular position be filled by a Francophone or an Anglophone, and not on the basis of merit, and further, that bilingualism, the law of the land, is not good enough, amounts in my considered opinion to racism. I call on members of the NAC board to reject Mayor Legere's regrettable remarks totally.

subsubtopic: CENTENNIAL OF ESTABLISHMENT OF MUNICIPAL PARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1988 is an important year for municipal parks. It was 100 years ago, in 1888, that the Ontario Legislature passed the first ever Public Parks Act in Canada. That same year the first municipal park was established. On September 3, 1888, the City of Port Arthur, now Thunder Bay, established the first Board of Parks Management in Canada. It also established Waverly Park, the first municipal park in Canada, in that year.
We should all share in the centennial celebrations of Thunder Bay. Without municipal parks we would not have the facilities for sport, recreation, culture and horticulture that we enjoy today in our cities and towns. I salute the City of Thunder Bay and its Parks and Recreation Department, indeed, all Parks and Recreation Departments across this great nation, for their commitment to municipal parks.
The Government of Canada can help municipalities and their parks by agreeing to put money in the Budget this year for municipal rebuilding programs.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-USE OF TISSUE FROM ABORTED FETUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, medical technology is such that it is now possible to use tissues and organs from aborted human fetuses for transplant purposes. Examples are pancreas cells for the treatment of diabetes, bone marrow, and organs such as kidneys. The recent Supreme Court decision on abortion leaves a void in the law governing these matters and might well lead to the deliberate growing of babies to be killed and used for spare parts, and a whole transplant industry based on fetal tissue technology.
The ethical, moral, and legal questions arising therefrom cannot continue to be set aside, and Parliament must prepare itself to deal with this issue.

subsubtopic: MEMORANDUM OF VICE-PRESIDENT OF OPERATIONS-JOB SECURITY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, disgraceful is the word for the internal memo, dated January 11, 1988, sent by Mr. Fletcher, senior vice-president of CN operations in which he asked regional authorities to finish their employment cuts so as to get them out of the way before a federal election. Here in Ottawa, we are all familiar with the problems of railway services in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. We realize that the railways are part of our essential services and must be maintained for the sake of regional economic development. We therefore have a duty to protect our admissible CN workers in Senneterre and the region.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that under the provisions of Bill C-85 passed six months ago, workers may not negotiate job security or any other issues. Since there still has been no arbitration nearly six months later, how will these workers be able to protect their jobs, considering CN's memo?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary State for External Affairs implied that I would go to Haiti with the delegation of Canadian parliamentarians. I want to state that the Hon. Member does not have the right to speak on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada. I may remind the House that we do not approve of this visit to Haiti and that we reserve the right not to take part in the visit at this time.
However, the Liberal Party of Canada has agreed to take part in the committee's proceedings next week, when we shall be considering and reviewing Canadian aid programs for Haiti, to determine whether they meet the needs and aspirations of the Haitian people.
We have also agreed to take part, the week after, in public hearings to be held in Montreal, where five members of the committee will hear the views of the Haitian community in Montreal, as well as the views of representatives of various non-governmental organizations working in Haiti.

subsubtopic: WAGE GAP BETWEEN MALE AND FEMALE WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1967 Statistics Canada began collecting data on the wage gap between men and women. Figures then showed that women were earning 58.4 per cent of what men were earning. According to the latest StatsCan report, women are now earning 66 per cent of a man's wage. That is hardly an impressive victory for women.
Last spring the Human Rights Commission called upon the federal Government to introduce a pay equity law with some teeth, a law to force employers to pay equal wages and not just to file reports. It has been eight months since the Commission made its recommendation and the Conservative Government has yet to respond.
Effective pay equity legislation requires mandatory compliance and insists on strong enforcement mechanisms to make it work. It must be bolstered by the support systems which encourage women to enter non-traditional occupations. These support systems include training and retraining programs for women, educational opportunities, and access to affordable, quality child care. Women can be assured of a bright future if the Government has the political will to put these systems in place.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and other Commonwealth heads of Government met in Vancouver and Lake Okanagan in October they agreed on measures to fight apartheid in South Africa and established a committee of foreign Ministers to give impetus to their decisions. 1 have the honour to chair that committee. 1 was asked in the House before departing by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellette) to report to the House, and I rise now to report to the House on the first meeting of that committee earlier this week in Lusaka, Zambia. In beginning, I want to express formally Canada's great appreciation of the excellent arrangements made by the Government of Zambia.
The committee comprises the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, Guyana, India, Nigeria, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. At Vancouver, the United Kingdom decided not to be a member of the committee, although Britain is contributing to other parts of the Commonwealth program against apartheid. For example, Britain and Canada will be
Statements by Ministers
the major contributors to the restoration of the second phase of the Limpopo Rail Line in Mozambique. Britain, Tanzania, Zimbabwe and Malawi are involved in the equally important work of providing security for transportation corridors against terrorist disruption. The best prospect for an end to apartheid is the negotiating concept developed by the Eminent Persons Group, established by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and other Commonwealth leaders in Nassau in the Bahamas. Our committee will work conscientiously to encourage conditions where that negotiating concept might be given effect.
Let me refer to the campaign to defend apartheid, Sir. It is systematic, organized, prosecuted as a priority by the Government of South Africa and supported, for various motives, by businesses and organizations with substantial interests in that country. Among some within South Africa, the resistance to change is intensified by fear, including the fear that they will be torn up from their own roots and that the strong economy they have created will be destroyed. That combination of power and fear is formidable, both in itself, and in the reaction it inspires.
Whatever other lessons might be learned from Africa, the record is consistent that, when majority rule could not be negotiated, it came by violence, fueled by the frustrations of majorities who would not forever be denied citizenship in their own country. That is the lesson of, among others, Kenya, Algeria, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. If the white 14 per cent of the population which governs South Africa maintains its racist system, the black majority will respond, inevitably, not with silence but with violence.
We have to take account of both the power and the fear that fuel apartheid. When I met President Chissano of Mozambique in August, he tried to address the understandable fear of white South Africans. He said:
The Afrikaaner is as African as I am. We both belong here. There is no
other place to which we can return.
The African National Congress acted in the same spirit in the meeting in Dakar, Senegal, where white and black South Africans came together to talk about their future together. Zimbabwe itself, with three white Ministers in the Government, and thousands of white citizens involved fully in industry, agriculture and the public service, is proof that white and black Africans can work together in freedom. The Commonwealth, because of our special reach across races and around the world, can help ease fears, among both blacks and whites. And Canada, in these circumstances, with our history and our nature, can play a leading role.

But fear is only one element of apartheid: power is another-power defended zealously, exercised ruthlessly.
Sanctions are applied for two purposes-the first economic; the second psychological. There is no doubt that the actions actually taken by Canada and other countries have sent clear messages of disapproval to defenders of apartheid, and of

February 5, 1988
Statements by Ministers
encouragement to its opponents. Nor is there doubt that the economic measures have inspired a vigorous campaign to bust sanctions, or evade them, or frustrate their purpose.
Naturally, the South African government does that; but so may other governments, so do many businesses. Those actions deserve to be known and, at Lusaka, we authorized terms of reference for two major studies which will bring to light new patterns of trade, new practices of accounting, new routings of shipments.
The terms of reference of the larger study have been published, and I have tabled them today. In the same spirit we are concerned by what appear to be significant breaches of the mandatory embargo on arms export, which members of the United Nations are obliged to respect. As individual nations, and as a committee, we will be seeking hard evidence and considering specific actions to ensure that the mandatory arms embargo is enforced.
The most effective new weapon enlisted in the defence of apartheid is the deliberate new emphasis on censorship within South Africa and propaganda at home and internationally. A simple summary of major press legislation in South Africa which sets out what journalists may not write about runs to over 300 pages. On top of that is the weight of other threats and regulations which limit freedoms that we Canadians take for granted: the freedom to meet, to publish, to speak without fear, and the right to protection against detention without trial.
No one knows how many people are detained today without charge in South Africa. No one who is detained knows when he or she might be freed or detained again. Even little children are locked away.
As the curtain comes down within South Africa, the campaign intensifies outside to portray as reform proposed institutions in which no authentic black leader will participate, to caricature all opponents of apartheid as communists or killers, to exploit prejudice. I have no doubt that the campaign of censorship and propaganda is carefully organized and targeted, and the Commonwealth will become much more involved in exposing and countering propaganda and censorship.
That holds its own risks. When it comes to rights, no Commonwealth country is blameless, some less than others. During the meeting in Lusaka and in other conversations, I warned that the accusation of a double standard would almost certainly be made against the Commonwealth and that the best way to deal with it is by improvement in our own countries, but most in this House and most in the world would agree that inequity or abuse in other countries does not excuse an apartheid regime which writes racism into law.
There is one other dimension of this committee which 1 want to convey to the House. We are eight countries from five continents. None of us is a superpower. Some, like Guyana, are states with profound economic problems of their own, while others of the front line states are vulnerable every day to destabilization from South Africa. That we came together gave evident hope to groups like the South African Council of Churches whose representatives we met.
What we can do together will enlarge the information and initiative and will to fight apartheid in peaceful and practical ways. That we are together is the best answer to the fear that is at the heart of apartheid, the fear that different races, different colours, cannot work together. The Commonwealth is the antithesis of apartheid. We are different races, different colours, working together. I expect that this committee will help us continue our progress.

subsubtopic: MEETING OF COMMONWEALTH FOREIGN MINISTERS, COMMITTEE IN LUSAKA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEETING OF COMMONWEALTH FOREIGN MINISTERS, COMMITTEE IN LUSAKA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Minister for providing me in advance with a copy of his statement. I wish also to congratulate him for rising in the House at the first opportunity to give us an account of this first meeting, held in Lusaka, Zambia, of the Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers which has been set up to initiate policies to fight against apartheid in South Africa. Unfortunately, this morning, he could not announce to the House very significant progress. He could only pay lip service to this very important cause. As he admitted himself on page 3 of his statement, and I quote:
The best prospect for an end to apartheid is the negotiating concept developed by the Eminent Persons Group-
Well, 1 must remind him that according to his Department's 1986-87 Annual Report, this initiative has not brought about the expected results. It is even described as a ... The document does not say so in so many words, but it implies that this initiative was ultimately a failure. I was surprised this morning when I heard the Minister refer to it.
Also, and this may be the most important and straightforward point of his whole statement, the Minister described the campaign to defend apartheid, and I quote:
This campaign to defend apartheid is:
-Systematic, organized, prosecuted as a priority by the Government of South Africa, and supported, for various motives, by businesses and organizations with substantial interests in that country.
To clarify this resistance, he points out further on:
Nor is there doubt that the economic measures have inspired a vigorous campaign to bust sanctions, or evade them, or frustrate their purpose.
It therefore seems obvious to me that, in spite of all our goodwill and all our efforts throughout the years, the situation in South Africa remains unchanged. The South African Government does not want to change its policies for any consideration or reason.
February 5, 1988

To relate to my own personal experience, I recall my first speech as Parliamentary Secretary to the Eton. Mitchel Sharp, then Secretary of State for External Affairs, before the UN General Assembly, in which I denounced apartheid. This was my first speech on behalf of Canada before the UN General Assembly, and I dealt with apartheid.
Today, 18 years later, I find myself still denouncing apartheid in this Elouse. This is why 1 can accept that Canada, through its Minister, should continue to play a role in cooperation with Commonwealth countries or South Africa's neighbours in an effort to put as much pressure as possible on South Africa, but I also believe that, apart from such efforts, which are praiseworthy and should be pursued, Canada must do more. I believe that Canada must now take drastic action.
At this point I think I should quote my Party Leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), who said, in an important speech:
Our goal as Liberals has always been to reach the day when every person on this planet lives under a rule of law which fully respects the human rights of all citizens. We can cite human rights abuses in every part of the globe, but nowhere are human rights being so blatantly trampled than by the institutionalized, state-sponsored racism of the apartheid regime in South Africa.
Last September, I called on our Government to impose complete economic sanctions and withdraw diplomatic relations from that country by the end of the year if no progress was made toward ending apartheid. That deadline has been passed, and again we demand that the Mulroney Government take action.
It is time for Canada to chart its own course, and send a clear message. Apartheid is an affront to human dignity and Canadians will not give validity to a regime which imposes it. I also believe that while it is preferable that we convince our allies to take the same action in concert with us, we must be prepared to act alone if need be.

This kind of dramatic gesture can have a very important psychological impact. It can act as a catalyst and help end a situation more quickly. I remember how Canada ventured forth on unbeaten paths in the early seventies when it recognized Mainland China, how it paved the way for many other western countries, how it in fact led the United States to do likewise, and how Canada's attitude, its unique position, enabled it to play a significant and important role on the international scene. I believe that today, breaking off diplomatic relations with South Africa would be as important and have the same impact as our decision, at the time, to be among the first to recognize the People's Republic of China.
I therefore urge the Conservative Government, as the Leader of our Party has done before, to make the dramatic gesture that would make it abundantly clear that we can no longer tolerate apartheid in South Africa.

subsubtopic: MEETING OF COMMONWEALTH FOREIGN MINISTERS, COMMITTEE IN LUSAKA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to begin by thinking the Right Hon. Minister for being
Statements by Ministers
faithful to Parliament and using the House rather than a press conference to report on his visit. It is greatly appreciated and a habit I hope other Ministers will imitate more frequently than they sometimes do.
In his statement the Minister made several points that I wish to comment on. The campaign to defend apartheid is rightly referred to as "systematic, organized and prosecuted as a priority by the Government of South Africa". The Minister went on to say, "supported for various motives by businesses and organizations with substantial interests in that country". Might I suggest-and I do not mean this in a narrow partisan way because it makes the Minister's approach to South Africa even more laudable in the circumstances-that one of the obvious, and I sometimes think willing, intellectual victims of this systematic campaign is the international conservative community, at least as expressed through its magazine International Conservative Insight, the latest issue of which 1 recommend to the Minister. That issue is a pot-pourri of attacks on sanctions, various anti-apartheid leaders, and approaches to the issue which the Minister himself condemns in his statement when he quite rightly denounces as propaganda the caricature offered by the South African Government and its propagandists of all opponents of apartheid as communists or killers.
The Minister has a lot of work to do in the broader political and ideological community to which he and his Party belong, and we wish him well. We also wish for him the same clarity of mind and language that he displays with respect to South Africa when it comes to the caricatures which come out of the Pentagon and White House concerning Central America and those in that region who want to control their own destiny. They are often referred to as communists or killers when neither description is appropriate.
The Minister says that if the white 14 per cent maintains its racist system, "the black majority will respond, inevitably, not with silence but with violence." With respect, that is all that the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) was saying when she was so roundly criticized by the Minister in September of 1987.

The Minister said, and rightly so, that the impact of sanctions is both economic and psychological. I applaud the concept of two studies on the ways and means used to avoid the impact of these sanctions. However, I suggest that these and other studies should also look into statements that some sanctions have actually reinforced certain sectors of the South African economy.
These statements made by opponents to sanctions must be addressed so that the effect of sanctions can be improved, if necessary, thus strengthening instead of weakening their impact.

February 5, 1988
Introduction of Bills

The Minister referred to the fact that even little children are locked away. In this respect, I met not too long ago with Ms. Ann Mitchell, Executive Director for Canada of the International Defence and Aid Fund for South Africa, who attended an international conference on children, repression and the law in apartheid South Africa. One of the recommendations coming out of that conference included the need to make known world-wide the plight of apartheid's child victims and the nature of the South African legal system, one primary purpose of which includes detention, arrest and imprisonment of children. I hope this is something that the Minister and the committee he chairs had in mind when they made their decision to counter South African propaganda, and that making known the plight of these children would be one of the things they would be following up.
I also hope that some day soon either the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade or the Standing Committee on Human Rights might have a chance to hear testimony about this from Canadians who attended that conference, or other Canadians who have concerned themselves with this particular matter. I know that is something they are hoping to be able to do.
I also had the opportunity to meet not so long ago with members of a Canadian delegation to Angola sponsored by the Canadian Council for International Co-operation. One of their principal recommendations was that Canada begin to treat Angola on a par with other front line States and SADCC countries. I am somewhat disappointed that the Minister did not take this opportunity to indicate any new Canadian policy with respect to those recommendations made by Canadian NGOs. I believe Canadian aid to the front line states has to be comprehensive, include all the countries that need that kind of aid, and be thorough. I encourage the Minister to work with the NGO community in Canada which is to co-operate with him in any efforts the Government might contemplate to increase both the amount and effectiveness of Canadian aid to all the front line states.
Finally, the Minister referred to the argument about a double standard and, in very careful language, talked about no Commonwealth country being blameless with regard to "rights". It may be incidental and have no consequence, but I am curious about the blanket use of the term "rights" rather than "human rights". The concession by the Minister that Canada is not blameless is interesting and I welcome it. I have the suspicion that had I got up in the House and said this about Canada the Minister may not have been so forthcoming.
However, the Minister is right in reminding those countries, some of which are strident in denouncing South Africa and its apartheid system but which are not exactly models of political tolerance themselves, to clean up their own houses in order that their criticisms of racism in South Africa might have even
more moral force than they already have by virtue of the inherent offence against humanity which apartheid constitutes.
The Commonwealth is the antithesis of apartheid, as the Minister has said. I might also suggest that la Francophonie, another organization to which Canada belongs in which both blacks and whites work together for the common good of the communities which they represent and the world, is also the antithesis of apartheid.
I ask the Minister to consider, not only with respect to the Commonwealth but also with respect to the U.N. and other international opportunities which Canada has in general, how Canada might act in concert with others and also alone to provide leadership and to give expression to the offence which Canadians unanimously, I hope, take to apartheid.
One of my colleagues has suggested some dramatic action. I do not agree with the dramatic action which he has suggested, the breaking off of all relationships with South Africa. That is not the policy which the NDP supports at this time. However, I do not think the Minister should rule out, as he sometimes does in his language, the possibility that some day-and I do not mean a far away day which never comes-we find ways for Canada to act alone and dramatically which would give expression to the unanimity with which Canadians abhor apartheid.
