speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak to Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. Although the constituency of Spadina has large railway yards in the southern end of the constituency, there is a very particular concern raised in the last several years and continuing into this year about rail safety that relates to the Gault line which runs along the northern boundary of Spadina and, in fact, runs east to west through the heart of the City of Toronto and Metro Toronto. Therefore, I am very much concerned not only because of the railway workers, the passengers, and so on, who are concerned with the railway yards in the south near the lake, but because of the situation on the Gault line about which 1 will say more.
In approaching this subject, I am concerned about the situation as reflected in the comments of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) this morning. In the last five years there were well over 300 fatalities in rail accidents. I am also concerned about the situation which has arisen just this year that because of failure of co-ordinated planning by the Government there is now no investigatory body since January 1 to look into rail accidents. The Government's own legislative action has cancelled the Railway Transport Commission and the Railway Transport Committee despite warnings by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the New Democratic Party. That rather supports the impression that the Government is not very serious about rail safety.
We are glad the Government is introducing legislation. Our Party and its predecessor have been asking for this for five decades. However, we are very sorry the legislation which was introduced is so weak that it is almost an excuse for no legislation. There are almost no teeth in it. The teeth will have to be in the regulations over which, of course, this Parliament and the public have no control, sometimes not even clear knowledge, and so far there has been no opportunity to debate them. If the Government will bring those regulations before the Standing Committee on Transport there will be at least some opportunity for Members of Parliament, including the opposition Parties and, I hope, the public, to examine those regulations and to give the Government the benefit of whatever wisdom they have. In that connection, I would hope particularly that all of the railway unions will be invited to comment on the regulations before they go into effect, since those people are the ones who must carry them out. In many cases, those people are the ones whose lives are most directly endangered by safety hazards.
In this connection, I want to say that it is not true, as has been implied by some people, that the principal failure of rail safety is the negligence of employees. There are other causes which often go unnoticed or, at least, they are not well publicized. I remember many years ago when my father, a lawyer in Winnipeg, took a case for a railway worker in a nearby town whose daughter had been killed on a railway siding. She had been going to school over a path used by herself and others for weeks during that winter and one day
she was crushed between two boxcars that were being shunted. What the court found was that the railway was fundamentally at fault. The regulations required that there be a "brakie" on the leading end of the car being shunted, but management, in its usual corner-cutting, cost-cutting, way neglected to put a brakie on that job. It saved a little money but it cost a little girl her life.
From my own experience of working 18 years in a factory, I know there are many accidents which occur not primarily through employee negligence but through unsafe conditions created by management, including conditions of speed-up- "Hurry, hurry, hurry. Get it done. Skip the little rules in the book if they slow down your work". Therefore, I am very deeply distressed that this Act provides a ratio of five government officials, who do not necessarily know what is going on with respect to the rail lines, and five railway representatives to one representative of the workers. There would be five representatives from the company which is interested in making profits, five representatives from the Government, but only one representative from the workers who must carry out the orders and whose lives, are themselves more at risk than the lives generally speaking, of the public. This is a very unfair imbalance. It puts a single worker representative in the position of being a mere token who can very often have no real influence on a decision for which he, nevertheless, might be held responsible along with the majority.
Another unfairness of this Bill is the scale of fines. We are told the maximum fine for a worker who violates this Act would be $10,000. However, the maximum fine for a company in violation would be $50,000. That is sickening. An amount of $10,000 could very well be 20 per cent or 25 per cent of the annual earnings of, say, a locomotive engineer. What about the annual earnings of the President of CPR which are about $600,000? For him, $10,000 is almost invisible. It is less than 20 per cent of his earnings. Not, of course, that he would be charged individually, but it does help to point out the contrast. The real contrast is with the annual profits of these companies, which I believe are never less than $100 million, at least on average. If the annual profit of the company is $100 million or more, and if there were to be a proportionate fine levied against the company when the company is at fault under this law, it should be in the range of $20 million to $30 million. That would be "a fine in proportion to the $10,000 against a locomotive engineer earning $40,000 or $50,000 a year.
The Government is not serious in this legislation about compelling or even persuading the companies to be serious about safety. Some of my colleagues have already pointed out the great lack of safety across this country at level crossings, for example. We have them in Toronto. The railways are very unwilling to spend a dollar, if they can avoid it under the law, in order to promote safety for children going to school and old people going to the store, or whatever else people have to do when they use level crossings.
There is a further unfairness in this Bill in its treatment of the doctor-patient relationship. This is something I have had
February 5, 1988

experience with during my 18 years in a factory. There was a company doctor. We were not required to go to the company doctor when we felt sick, but we were required to go to the company doctor when they wanted us examined. The company doctor considered it his obligation to give the medical information to the company. Why? Because the company paid his fee. In ordinary business terms, of course, you get what you pay for and you give what you are paid for. However, the College of Physicians and Surgeons has a different view. The view of the College of Physicians and Surgeons, as expressed to the Toronto Board of Health some years ago in a letter, when we asked its view on a safety question and on a question of a doctor's responsibility to the patient, including a company doctor, said that the only person entitled to receive the information about the patient's health from the doctor is the patient or anyone to whom the patient is willing to have the information transmitted. He must give his waiver before that information is given to anyone else, whether it is the company, the union, the police or whoever it is. That is the view of the College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Yet this Bill violates the traditional confidential relationship between doctor and patient by stating that the doctor must give information on the patient's health to the employer. There may be a ground for an employer needing to know certain facts about the patient's condition. It can be addressed, but it should not be addressed simply by an arbitrary rule that the doctor can tell the employer whatever he thinks he should tell him and that the patient should have no recourse against that.
What has happened in our factory is that sometimes the doctor gave information to the employer that he had not even given to the patient. The patient did not know his own condition fully. I know that in another factory in Toronto, a lead factory, the doctor withheld vital information about lead contamination in the employees' bodies.
He may have given the information to the company but he withheld it from the patients because he considered that his obligation was to the people who paid him his money and not to the person whose life he was examining and to whom as a doctor he was sworn to be responsible.
Therefore I find that this pattern in the legislation of reducing worker representation on the railway safety code consultative committee to a token, and of setting such an unfair balance of fines and of giving the company rights over the information regarding the patient's life when he has been examined by a doctor, information which even the patient may not have, I find those to be in the pattern of blaming the workers in a situation where costs are cut on safety so that the profit goes to the company and the personal risk of injury and the blame goes to the worker. That is far too common a pattern in our country. I am sorry that this Bill perpetuates it.
It does thereby give to the company an incentive to increase its profits by corner-cutting. As has been pointed out, the
Railway Safety Act
Government has given the companies another kind of incentive to do the same thing by introducing deregulation. It has made Canadian Pacific and Canadian National extremely vulnerable to unfair competition from south of the border given the geographic arrangements. But to add this further incentive of giving the company an unfair control over safety decisions as against the workers is going to mean that companies will spend even less money on the construction or maintenance of tracks, even less money on the removal of level crossings, even less money on the buying of safety equipment and the maintaining of it in safe running order, even less money on adequate training for all employees, and even less money on necessary scheduling of employees' time so that there is no danger of overtiredness on the job. I think that is very unfortunate. There are possibilities that the Bill's faults in this respect can be rectified. I hope that the government Members as well as the opposition Members will look for those faults and remedy them in amendments in the Transport Committee.
I want to mention one other matter to which I referred at the beginning. Last month the Toronto Area Rail Transportation of Dangerous Goods Advisory Council held hearings in Toronto concerning the complaints that arose about danger on the Gault line since the notorious railway derailment in Mississauga in 1979. There has been continuous and strong pressure from residents of Toronto to stop the practice of bringing dangerous goods, explosives or dangerous gasses, anything that could cause harm to human beings as well as property if railway cars were derailed and perhaps broken open by the force of derailment. None of those things should be transported through that railway line.
At present about 80 percent of what goes through that railway line neither originates in Metro Toronto nor does it terminate in Metro Toronto. It is a through line for most of these dangerous goods. We are saying they should not be curried there. But there is nothing in this Bill that gives us anything to hang on to. Everything in it is referred, as it were, in a discretionary way. The vital parts are referred in a discretionary way to the regulations which we have not seen and do not know when we will see them.
The people in Toronto, and I do not mean just a few residents, I mean Toronto City Council and Metro Council, have both demanded that that line be moved out of Toronto, not on to the perimeter of Toronto but well north of Toronto, for which surveys have been done in a preliminary way. It is a feasible line to build. The advantage of it is that even though population in those areas will no doubt grow, even if the line is built now well outside of Toronto, there can be a buffer strip created along the line so that residents will not be living cheek by jowl with a railroad carrying dangerous goods. At present it would be horrendously costly to build a buffer strip such as that through the City of Toronto because there would be a great deal of expensive property that would have to be acquired. So we want the line out of Toronto.
I believe that from my knowledge of the housing and real estate activities in Toronto and Metro the cost of moving the

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
line would be fully recovered by the railway and its subsidiaries such as Marathon Realty because the land values would immediately soar. 1 know Marathon well enough to know it would make a mint of money out of recycling that railway line into housing.
1 regret that this law is weak as it is. It is no doubt better than nothing. It is a start. But it is a very poor start considering what the Government should have brought in in connection with public complaints. It gives no real voice to the workers. It gives no real voice to the public. It is loaded in favour of the cost-cutting interests of the companies.
I hope that this Bill will be amended so as to provide that the Government and the companies and the unions at least would sit down public hearings, to which the public have access as well, in order to work out a fairer system of responsibility for rail safety.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) on a question or comment.

The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has emphasized the lack of provisions for safety on the railways. By way of comment, I would like to point out to him the Canadian incident record of railway happenings, and I will read from a report which states that the number of train accidents, derailments, collisions, crossings and maintenance equipment accidents decreased from 1,456 to 985 or 32 per cent between 1975 and 1985.
The Hon. Member gives the impression that all across the transportation modes there will be a decrease of interest and concern for safety. May I point out again that the Hon. Minister has emphasized that safety and security will be a top priority in the deregulation aspect of the modes of transportation.
In the United States, and on the United States' side, I do not know why the Hon. Member feels that this record of safety will diminish. How does the Hon. Member respond to the position of John Riley, a federal railroad administrator in the United States where the Staggers Act and the deregulation policy have been implemented for several years ahead of that which is being implemented in Canada? Mr. Riley states, "One of the often overlooked aspects of this issue is that safety for the railroads has improved dramatically since Staggers". I think there is a direct cause and relationship there. There is no reason to believe that with deregulation safety will be prejudiced.
The Hon. Member makes the misconceived statement that the Bill has no provision for investigation of accidents on the railway. Bill C-105 refers to the National Transportation Act and a National Transportation Agency. If the Hon. Member reads that Act, he will realize that the responsibilities charged to that agency is one of investigating the reason for the
accident and determining causes, which gives Parliament an opportunity thereafter to take the necessary action.
As a Ministry, we have indicated that safety is of high priority as are the number of safety factors, security measures, and inspectors to ensure that the security measures are implemented and kept in place. I say to the Hon. Member that the basis of his presentation is not properly founded when he points out that safety will be prejudiced in the years to come under Bill C-105.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) for his intervention, and I take him quite seriously, knowing his concern in a number of other areas. I may not have explained myself clearly on one point that he raised. I did not intend to say that this Bill has no provision for investigation. If I stated that, I was mistaken. That was not what I meant to say. What I am referring to is the fact that for the last five weeks there is no provision for investigation. There is a gap. The accidents do not stop, but the investigation authority has stopped.
There I am referring to a statement attributed to L. R. Steves on January 19. He is the Atlantic District Director of NTA Rail Safety Branch. In chairing a public meeting in Halifax dealing with a series of derailments that have taken place in Nova Scotia over the past year or so, Mr. Steves admitted that as of January 19, there is no agency empowered to investigate accidents or make other inquiries into matters related to railway safety.
When this Bill is passed, and when the regulations are written and put into force, they may very well provide what the Hon. Member says. But sitting in front of the Hon. Member is a Minister whose colleague last summer promised a change of regulations in immigration matters. After six months all he does is to send us a nice letter saying that it will be some months yet before those regulations are written. We really do not know how long it will take to write the regulations for Bill C-105 and put them into effect. Until then, in effect, there is no investigative agency. We just have to hope that accidents will miraculously cease until the Government gets ready to put an agency back into being.
The Hon. Member referred to a decrease in the accident rate over a decade. I believe I remember that earlier today he referred to a decrease in the volume of traffic. Of course, one way to bring the accident rate to zero would be to shut down the railways entirely and permanently. Sometimes, in passenger traffic, it looks as if that is exactly what the railway companies are trying to do. If there is no service, there will be no passengers. Nobody will be hurt. There will be no workers, and none of them will be hurt either. I do not think that is what the Hon. Member who raised the question wishes, but I think his use of that statistic raises as many questions as it might answer.
As to the Minister's assurance that safety has a high priority, we have heard that before. We have heard it many
February 5, 1988

times. It is now more than eight years since the derailment in Mississauga. That derailment could have been a disaster with a disastrous death toll, if it had not happened in fairly vacant land. If that had happened north of Dupont Street in Spadina, there may have been hundreds of fatalities. We do not know. But certainly it would have been a much larger disaster. Yet eight years later the matter is still being investigated under the authority of the Minister. There is no big hurry about safety, Mr. Speaker. This is in spite of representations from the city council and from the metro council, both of which are led by responsible officials, many of them of the same Party as the Hon. Member who raised this question with me. Yet they cannot get a serious answer from the Government on the safety question.
Most people are not even satisfied that the 25 mile per hour limit is being observed. It is difficult to prove. If someone stands by a train that goes rushing by, they usually do not have a radar trap with them in order to test the speed of the train. I know that residents along that line do not believe that the railway is honouring its so-called voluntary undertaking to reduce speeds to 25 miles per hour when carrying dangerous goods.
The public in Toronto is becoming impatient waiting for some evidence that the Minister has this high regard for safety that we have been told about.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today on the Bill entitled, "An Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof1.
Since I came to the House in 1984, I have been a full and active member of the Transport Committee. During that time the committee has dealt with a number of pieces of transportation legislation. We have dealt with two deregulation Bills, the Aviation Safety Act, and the Canada Shipping Act. This Bill is clearly an important component. It exemplifies the Government's attitude towards safety that it was not in a position to bring in a rail safety Act until after it had not only brought in legislation dealing with deregulation on the railroads, but actually had that legislation enacted and in effect.
As we know, even if we move quickly, consideration of Bills like this will take time. It is regrettable that, up until this point, the Government has put safety on the back burner.
Let me begin by indicating why we need a Railway Safety Act. I should point out that rail unions since almost immediately after the Second World War, along with the CCF and then the NDP, have been calling for a Railway Safety Act. It goes to show that the previous administration did not value safety on the rails as a high priority, nor did previous Conservative Governments. However, I am pleased that we finally have a Bill before us. I look forward to the work that we will be doing in the Standing Committee on Transport to refine the
Railway Safety Act
legislation to reflect better the needs of the people who work on the rails and the people who come in contact with railroads.
I want to do a little historical look-see since 1984 and to start with the final piece of correspondence I have on a matter regarding inspection procedures, particularly in Thunder Bay but elsewhere as well. It is a letter addressed to the Minister of Transport from the Canadian Division, Brotherhood of Railway Carmen, signed by its National President, S. A. Horodyski. I want to read into the record parts of this letter. It was sent in response to a letter from the Minister saying that safety was no problem and that there was no need for a safety inquiry. It read:
Your response has missed the point of our concerns. Your policies have failed to recognize the serious potential for disaster being created by the railways' massive lay-offs of the employees who are responsible and specifically trained to identify defective railway rolling stock components and ensure they are set off the train and properly repaired prior to resumption of service.
The intervals of inspections by specially trained carmen (car inspectors) are being reduced drastically across Canada's railways with elimination of inspection points with the railways relying on unqualified personnel to insure safe movement of trains across Canada. This practice appears to have the blessing of the soon to be defunct Canadian Transport Commission (CTC)...
An example of why our confidence in the CTC is not what it should be is attached which deals with a directive by the CTC to CP Rail concerning mechanized inspections, which was ignored by the railway without any repercussion.
While technologies introduced on the railways today have assisted in reducing mechanical failures, they have not eliminated those failures. It is extremely precarious for railways to adopt an attitude towards safety which is on a practical basis as opposed to one based on a stringent standard of rail safety with consistent maximum application so as to ensure minimal failure, thereby, protecting against loss of life, personal injury of employees and the general public, as well as property damage.
By the federal Government introducing the economic regulatory reform (C-18) first, the railways appear to have taken this as a signal from the Government that safety takes second place to economics. This is further evidence by our understanding that the Railway Safety Act mentioned in your letter will not be introduced until sometime in 1990.
Obviously that part of the letter was incorrect, because the Act is before us in 1988.
I want to return to the reference about CPR ignoring CTC instructions. The matter was first raised with me in February 1986. To go back a little further, I have a May 24, 1985 copy of an internal CPR memo from the General Car Foreman addressed to the Westfort supervisors and the traffic yard supervisors in Thunder Bay. It reads:
Effective immediately, Kubota Tractors are to be utilized to perform train inspections at Westfort Yard.
This is to be done in all areas where the tractors can be driven and operated in a safe manner. It is realized that some areas are not yet suitable for this operation but will be made so in the future.
That was CP's first shot. On February 12, 1986 I received a letter from the President of Lodge 361, Mr. Lemesani of the Canadian Division of Brotherhood Railway Carmen. It read: Dear Mr. Angus:
The subject of this letter in the form of a petition, is that of the Safety Standing Inspection of originating trains in the Westfort Inspection Yard of

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
CP Rail by the Carmen who are being forced to do these inspections while operating Kubota tractors.
All Carmen of Lodge 361 in Thunder Bay who are required to do inspections of trains while driving the tractors, maintain that they can not do a proper inspection. Most of the under carriage is not visible while sitting on a tractor. The Carmen have to look ahead at the road while driving, and insist that no one can see to his side to inspect the train and also ahead to drive at the same time. This will undoubtedly cause many defects on these trains to be missed.
Many of these trains travel in excess of a thousand miles before having another Standing Inspection, and only have Pull-By inspections while on route to their destination. The Carmen of Thunder Bay strongly urge that this policy be changed, by allowing the qualified inspectors (Carmen) to walk the train while inspecting. In this manner they will be able to inspect cars properly by standing and bending to see up under the cars at the coupler assemblies, at the brake rigging and a close inspection of the wheels, all of which when defective cause cars to derail and cause major mishaps.
The lives of all the public who come in contact with these trains at level crossings and in towns and cities in which these trains travel through are at stake, as well as the train crews. The Carmen, who are the Safety Qualified Inspectors on the railroad know that they cannot inspect trains properly while driving tractors, and stress to you that this policy must be changed for the safety of all.
I wrote to the Minister of Transport at that time asking him to investigate the matter, which he did. On May 9, 1986, the then Minister of Transport, the present Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) wrote the following:
Dear Mr. Angus:
Thank you for your letter of 17 February 1986, with which you enclosed a copy of correspondence from Mr. H. Lemesani of Britannia Lodge No. 361 of the Brotherhood of Railway Carmen, concerning safety inspections at CP Rail's Westfort inspection yard at Thunder Bay.
I appreciate receiving Mr. Lemesani's comments on this matter. I understand that the Railway Transport Committee-was aware of this type of inspection practice. The matter was investigated and, as a result, the RTC instructed CP Rail to correct its practice.
I trust that this action will meet Mr. Lemesani's concerns. Thank you for your interest in this matter.
The practice was not corrected, and I have what appears to be a telex dated at Winnipeg on June 17, 1986 from the General Manager, Operation and Maintenance, CPR. It went to some of the Thunder Bay supervisors and read:
This refers to the recent press clipping from Thunder Bay and Moose Jaw quoting various Members of Parliament that CP Rail has been ordered by the Railway Transport Committee to cease using Kubota tractors in the safety inspection of freight cars. The procedures that CP Rail is using has been adopted by most North American railroads and we do not intend to back off from our position. You should therefore ensure that there will be no changes made in our inspection and repair procedures at Thunder Bay and Moose Jaw regardless of what the press has said.
Obviously regardless of what the Minister of Transport was saying at that time as well. This is why we need a Railway Safety Act. From January 24, 1986 to February 7, 1986, the following is a list of the level of inspections and what they found at Thunder Bay:
January 24-10 trains were run thru-only one was given a thorough check for running-gear defects train #481-Unit #5545 had skids reported on #5 and #6 wheels and had to be taken to the shops for repair. January 30-6 trains were run thru-only 1 was given a thorough running gear check . . .
February 1-7 trains R/T-only 1 checked-
February 3-6 trains R/T-2 checked-
February 7-7 trains R/T, 2 checked-
Obviously economics are dictating to the railroads that they must reduce their level of inspections. They are dropping back on the number of inspectors and changing work responsibilities for less qualified people to do the inspections, and all in the name of cutting costs. When they cut costs, they cut corners. This is also why we need a Railway Safety Act.
Quite frankly we need a Railway Safety Act which is a bit stronger than the one before us. Instead of there being an overseeing committee charged with the responsibility of administering the inspection side of things or in charge of enforcement, we have a railway safety consultative committee.
I mentioned earlier that this House had passed another Act during the life of this Government, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act. Under that Act there was not a consultative board or an advisory board set up. There was a Canadian Aviation Safety Board. Let me quote from that Act:
There shall be a board to be known as the Canadian Aviation Safety Board consisting of not fewer than three members, at least one of whom shall be a full-time member, to be appointed by the Governor in Council.
This Board is to oversee aviation safety, not observe it, not to pass comments to Ministers but to oversee it. Concerning the object of the Board, we find:
The object of the Board is to advance aviation safety
(a)	by identifying safety deficiencies as evidenced by aviation occurrences;
(b)	by conducting independent investigations and. if necessary, public inquiries into aviation occurrences in order to make findings as to their contributing factors and causes; and
(c)	by reporting publicly on its investigations and public inquiries and on the findings in relation thereto and by making recommendations designed to eliminate or reduce safety deficiencies.
What we have in the Railway Safety Act is:
The Minister may establish a committee, to be known as the Railway Safety Consultative Committee . .. consisting of not fewer than two and not more than four members who, in the opinion of the Minister, have special expertise or special interests in matters of safe railway operations, plus seven other members as follows:
(a)	one member to represent the Minister;
(b)	one member to represent the Canadian National Railway Company;
(c)	one member to represent Canadian Pacific Limited;
(d)	one member to represent VIA Rail Canada Inc.;
(e)	one member to represent the other railway companies to which this Act applies;
(f)	one member to represent the shippers of rail freight traffic; and
(g)	one member to represent the Canadian Railway Labour Association.
What does this committee do?
The Committee may, on its own initiative, and shall, at the request of the Minister, advise and make recommendations to the Minister on any matter affecting safe railway operations, and shall make to the Minister at least one report annually on the activities of the Committee.
That is not good enough at all. If we are to have a properly developed rail safety act, we have to ensure that we are not
February 5, 1988

allowing the bureaucrats in the Department or the Minister, although we accept the fact that ultimately the Minister is responsible for the safety of the railways, but an independent board with the power to oversee the activities of the rail safety act.
The other area of concern that I have and upon which some of my colleagues have touched already is that of fines. There is an incredible imbalance in this Bill. We do not have to go back too far, just to the Hinton inquiry, to hear about the pressures of the rail industry and how it has become the practice for a conductor to not stop a train because he cannot communicate with the head end-he assumes it is a radio problem or what have you-and, if the train is later he will probably get demerit points. So, that railway psychology came into being. Someone who perhaps breaks a rule, not vindictively, but because everyone else is, may become involved in an accident. This individual is subject to a fine of SI0,000. The company, which may have set the scenario for that ignoring of the rules by the economic pressure on workers-assuming that it could be convicted of that-will be fined $50,000.
Now, $50,000 to the CPR is petty cash, to use a phrase that was used earlier today. That is meaningless to the CPR, but $10,000 to an individual who works for the railroad, who is a brakeman, a conductor or an engineer with a family and a mortgage, is a lot of money. While there should be penalties for infractions, we have to keep the balance in mind. Quite clearly, the fine for the railroads the corporations, is peanuts. The amount should be raised substantially so that it is no longer deemed a licence fee, a licence fee to stretch safety requirements, to avoid living up to the law of the land.
The amount should be substantial. Make it $1 million, make it $5 million or make it $10 million. Obviously, we should be giving the judiciary the power to set a fine that relates to the infraction. If one of the two railroads providing locomotive services to VIA Rail, for example, by their economic action have not had locomotives safety checked for a period longer than is acceptable, and if they put at risk the lives of their passengers on that train, why should they only face a fine of $50,000 if convicted? It is ludicrous. That $50,000 has to be raised significantly. What about putting on a ceiling of $10 million or $20 million, but make the amount a major economic impact on the operator.
Another area to which I want to refer briefly is the section which requires engineers employed by a proposing party to certify for safety railway works that have received ministerial approval as well as other works which fall within certain prescribed categories. This section removes the responsibility of the regulator to ensure that works are completed to an acceptable standard for safe operation while placing that responsibility in the hands of proposing parties, namely, railway companies for the most part.
This provision of the Bill will make it easier for railway companies to operate as they choose. It is unclear what contribution they will make to safety of railway operations. I
Railway Safety Act
think it is a responsibility of the Government to ensure that whatever works are paid for meet the standards. The Government should not rely on the railroad or the company because they may cut corners. A company may decide to design something in a way that has a limited lifespan for purely economic reasons. That section has to be changed.
I am sure that if we talk to railroaders across the country we would be horrified to hear about all of the things happening, the violations and the stretching of safety, all of the problems that have been created in the name of the bottom line. Move more goods faster at less cost is the philosophy. There is a cost, and ultimately that cost is safety.
1 look forward to working with my colleagues on the Transport Committee in reviewing this legislation and hearing witnesses. Hopefully we can modify the Bill and make it better. We have to change the consultative committee to give it real power. We have to change the make-up because it is really a railroad company committee as it stands now, with weight behind it. We have to achieve some balance. Over the years the railroad workers themselves have been fighting for safety, whether health and safety for themselves, demanding changes in the lay-out of the locomotives so that the workers can work in a proper environment, or whether it is inspection procedures, track maintenance, you name it. The railroad workers are the ones who have been fighting. We have a responsibility to them to make sure that this Bill, which will probably not be amended for quite some time, is the best possible rail safety act that money can buy.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member. I always have considered him to be a reasonable Member, one who is trying to move the world forward with his comments and his positions. However, I was disturbed to hear him talk about the Government putting rail safety on the back burner.
As the Hon. Member knows, this piece of legislation is the first railway safety legislation of a comprehensive kind to be introduced in Canada in a long time. In fact, I am told that the original rail safety legislation was introduced in 1908, a long time ago. While there have been amendments and some tinkering with the law in an attempt to improve it in that time, there has not been a comprehensive look at the safety legislation until now, 1988, under the present Government.
I would hope that the Hon. Member would give credit where credit is due. This is a major step forward that has been long overdue and the credit for it belongs to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the present Government.
I know from the Hon. Member's comments that he will be working to improve the Bill. I think that is exactly what all of us should be doing. That is the main thrust of the railway safety legislation itself. Safety is of prime significance to the public as it is to all Hon. Members. Members of the public do not want to see us playing politics with safety. They want to

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
see us working together to make sure that railways and all other modes of transportation are as safe as they possibly can be.
1 might point out to the Hon. Member that there are some concerns about the speed with which this legislation is actually progressing. A consultative process took place in the development of the Bill and part of that consultative process was with the railways, the unions and citizen groups such as the M-TRAC organization from Metropolitan Toronto, Metro residents for rail safety. That group played a major part in the consultation in and development of the Bill and it is most concerned that it have an opportunity to examine the Bill in its final form carefully and to make representations before the committee because it has many concerns with the Bill. I hope the Hon. Member will agree to co-operate with that and will give his assurance that he and his Party are prepared to give every accommodation to citizen groups who wish to make representations-
Listen to him.
-and that in fact they will co-operate in ensuring that this Bill is the best possible Bill to ensure public safety on the railways.
They refused a hundred witnesses.
1 am sure the Hon. Member will not be disturbed by his colleague who keeps shouting out and interrupting me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank the Hon. Member for his comments and his questions. I will give credit to this Government. Unlike the last, it did bring in a rail safety Bill. The point, though, is the over-all priorities.
The Conservative Government has made its prime focus in transportation the economic side, deregulation. Bills C-18 and C-19, the deregulation Bills, were brought in well before the Railway Safety Act was brought in. It is my understanding that a national highway safety code is not in place yet. That code was to be in place to ensure that under deregulation, there was one set of national rules to govern trucking on the highways.
In road and rail, 1 can legitimately say that the Government had its priorities reversed. I will give credit to the Government because it dealt with safety on the air side before it deregulated it or deregulated it any more than the Liberals already had.
The Hon. Member spoke about M-TRAC, a very excellent organization. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that it was not the New Democrats who refused to allow in excess of 100 groups to appear before the Transport Committee studying Bills C-18 and C-19. We would be more than happy to hear from everyone who wishes to have input.
As I said in my speech, this is an important piece of legislation. The Hon. Member has pointed out that there has not been a comprehensive review of it since 1908. This means
that it will be some time in the next century before we do it again. Even though it might take us a bit of extra time, I think we should do it right this time.
I would ask government Members to go into this not with the Whip's hand at their backs but with open minds and open eyes to look legitimately at this legislation and make it the best possible. This is not a philosophical issue, it is a question of safety, safety for those who work on or beside the rails and safety for the public as well.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to participate briefly in the debate on Bill C-105, an Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof. This is indeed a comprehensive piece of legislation. It is several hundred pages long, indeed a Bill which warrants special attention by all Hon. Members.

Since as usual, the Official Opposition in the House is prepared to give its full co-operation, Mr. Speaker, we want the Government to promise to hold hearings and listen to what the people have to say about a subject as important as that of the safety of our Canadian railways.
Mr. Speaker, we know the Railway Act has not been amended for many years. That is why it would be important for parliamentarians, as I said earlier, to hear the voice of the people, of elected municipal officials and of a large number of Canadians who are interested in the subject, and also of course, the voice of the railway unions.

This piece of legislation is necessary to bring rail standards up to date. It moves in the right direction and to that extent, of course, the Liberal Party intends to offer its usual co-operation to ensure that the Bill goes to committee without delay.
Sit down then.
The Hon. Member across said that I should sit down. It only takes a Tory to make those kinds of unfortunate and Tory-like remarks-
Ignorant remarks.

As my distinguished colleague from York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) has said, ignorant. That is a good way to describe it. We do not apologize for being concerned with railway safety. It is an important issue for us and it is important for me as a Member who represents a constituency in which there is a very important railway line which faced closure because of the inaction and unfortunate decisions of this Government to cut back on rail services.
Notwithstanding attempts of government Members to scuttle debate, I will continue with the brief remarks I had in mind. Statistics for the year 1985 from the Canadian Transport Commission show that 59 people died in rail-related
February 5, 1988

accidents and 400 people suffered bodily injuries. One must wonder just how many more Canadians were affected because, of course, not all rail-related accidents are reported and for that matter, not all accidents of any kind are reported.
We know, of course, that the Foisy report was tabled in January of 1987. It has had a major impact on bringing rail safety to the attention of Canadians. A number of the recommendations of the Foisy report are in place now or are in this Bill.
There is a concern shared by some people that the Minister responsible for railways is also going to be responsible for rail safety. That is not a conflict of interest, but it is a form of conflict. We just wonder how sincere a Minister can be about the responsibility for rail safety when the same Minister is responsible for deregulation. We know about the adverse impact deregulation can have on rail safety. Need we remind ourselves of the experiments in highway transport deregulation and airline deregulation in the U.S. and the impact it had there. While not saying deregulation of Canadian railways will necessarily cause a number of accidents, we have to be conscious of the fact that when you operate in a deregulated environment you at least increase the chances of mishaps. Therefore, the concern for safety has to be increased in order to compensate for the danger inherent in the deregulation process.
The Minister has been telling the railways to downsize. We know about internal correspondence between officials of railways and railway employees with respect to cut-backs and how they are supposed to go about it. 1 have an article written by Mr. Lome Slotnick of The Globe and Mail. Seeing as it comes from that newspaper, 1 know the Ministers here today will pay close attention because it is a very factual and accurate article, as I am sure they know. It says:
A senior executive of Canadian National Railways has ordered his managers to get moving quickly on layoffs and other "downsizing" because the Crown corporation will find it harder to do so during an election campaign.
"Current opinion is reflecting the strong possibility of a late spring-early summer federal election,"-
That was before the latest round of scandals. We know the possibility is a little more remote now. To continue:
-says a confidential internal memo, dated Jan. 11, from D. L. Fletcher, CN's senior vice-president for operations. "Downsizing actions may be harder to implement as this time approaches."
So we have a situation whereby decisions on downsizing and lay-offs which could affect rail safety are taken not necessarily because they are the appropriate decision at this time, but because it is politically expedient to do so now as opposed to some months from now.
We all know that CN Rail has plans to shut down a large number of rail lines. The effect of doing so will not only be on rail safety but highway safety as well. 1 may have brought to your attention before the fact that CN has produced an
Railway Safety Act
internal document, a copy of which I just happen to have here because someone slid it underneath my door one day, which demonstrates clearly the intention of CN to shut down a number of rail lines across Canada, some of which are in the great constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
The document I have comes from the St. Lawrence region of CNR and contains a rationalization program, which is a euphemism for cut-backs, from 1986 to 1996. It is entitled, "Lists of Sections Identified for Abandonment". Among those sections are the Beachburg subdivision, 163.9 miles, and the Alexandria subdivision, some 57.7 miles. That subdivision is the part of the CN rail line between Ottawa and Montreal. Actually, it runs from the Quebec border just west of Coteau-Station. I know the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) is familiar with that area. It runs from there almost to Ottawa. In other words, through my constituency. If you put the Beachburg subdivision together with the Alderdale subdivision, it would mean rail transport between Montreal and Sudbury could be done only via Toronto if one is using the CN line.
Why is that important to rail safety? For a number of reasons. I see my friend from York East is here. I know he is interested in the subject of transportation of dangerous goods via Toronto. He will know that once you shut down this rail line from Sudbury to Montreal, you increase the traffic and the flow of dangerous goods through Toronto. That is where the other line is. I have discussed this with the Hon. Member before and I know he is concerned about the issue. I congratulate the Hon. Member for his interest.
1 have another letter here dated September 9, 1986, from the office of the President and Chief Operating Officer of CN rail. I do not think he likes me reading his confidential letters here in the House but that is just tough. It says:
This will confirm discussions on Thursday, September 4. 1986, concerning the Alderdale-Beachburg Subdivisions.
You will remember that is the line between Ottawa and Sudbury. He goes on:
These changes in routing should achieve economies of scale in the Montreal-Toronto corridor, and at the same time, will focus attention on actively seeking alternatives for handling the 2,000 annual carloads of woodpulp traffic from Portage du Fort, which is currently served by way-freight from Ottawa.
A carload is the equivalent of about two large 18-wheelers. This means 4,000 extra truckloads of wood pulp could be placed on the road in the national capital area as a result of that line closure. Obviously when you talk about rail safety there is a parallel concern about an increase in truck traffic which in turn increases the chances of accidents on the highways. We know that transporting goods by truck has a lower safety record than by rail. That is quite normal. We are talking about transporting on highways which become slippery during harsh periods of winter which does cause that unfortunate circumstance. That is an entire area which is not necessarily discussed in this Bill at all. However, that is an area of real safety which I want to bring to the attention of the Government.

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
I know that the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) is interested in the area of transportation of dangerous goods. Chemicals produced in northern Ontario presently go through the Alderdale, Beachburg, and Alexandria subdivisions. If the unfortunate decision to close this line were ever implemented, those goods would be shipped to Montreal via Toronto. In the process those dangerous goods would be travelling through an area with an even greater concentration of population, thereby further compromising the safety of Canadians.
I bring those matters to the attention of the House, not in an effort to use up time or delay the passage of this Bill, but to bring to the attention of the Government and all Members who will sit on the committee studying Bill C-105 that in the area of rail safety there is an important concern about safety on the tracks and the downsizing measures and cut-backs forced by the Government which may affect safety on those tracks.
A second concern is the effects which deregulation could have on rail safety. There are other concerns which I have expressed which I will summarize again in conclusion. Those are my concerns in the area of downsizing railroads and shutting down rail lines which will increase truck traffic and further compromise the safety of Canadians.
I wish to offer my own co-operation and that of my colleagues. I hope that the Government and all Members who will be sitting on the committee will take into consideration the remarks I have just made in order to ensure that rail lines are not closed, creating safety concerns in addition to the ones we have already. It is a difficult area to deal with.
I know that Governments are trying to cut down on rail lines but a cut-back in rail lines is not necessarily an economy. In many cases the federal Government saves a few dollars, but the increased truck traffic on highways causes further deterioration of road-beds. In that case you achieve an economy for the federal Government but an expense for the provinces which are charged with maintenance of highways. That is an important concern which I hope the Tories will remember.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my hon. friend. I listened to his speech and I do not think he mentioned in any detail the fact that the Bill contains no provision to allow employees to relate unsafe practices. In other words, when they encounter unsafe practices or are asked to do something which they believe is unsafe or unsound in terms of health or safety, there is no provision in the Bill for their protection.
Does my hon. friend not think it is reasonable that legislation should contain some mention of how that is to be handled? If employees are expected to report on unsafe practices by their superiors, it would be like reporting on your boss. That is probably an unfair request to make of any employee unless there was a procedure for the avoidance of any possible harassment. Could my hon. friend comment on those two items?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for his question. The Hon. Member is right in that there is nothing to encourage or protect an employee who may decide to report or make public or inform his superiors or supervisors of a deficiency in the railway safety system. Obviously, an employee should be encouraged as much as possible to do so, and there should be a special provision in the Act or the regulations to protect the employee in question. In fact, this is not the only part of the Bill that is found wanting in this respect.
For instance, we know that a committee will be created as a result of this Bill. I have been told the committee will have eleven members: Four will be ministerial appointments, six will be appointed by the railway companies, and only one will be appointed by the unions.
So as you see, Mr. Speaker, we hardly have a balanced situation here. One representative for the workers and ten for the Department and the railways.
I think it is clear that this particular clause, I believe it is Clause 44, should provide a better balance, that is, increased representation by those who speak for the railway workers. I think the Government would do well to have a larger number of employees so that these employees or more appropriately, their representatives, the unions, could raise any concerns they might have about safety or similar subjects.
Interestingly, there are a number of other groups that do not have much say in the matter either. 1 am thinking of groups representing community interests, and a good example would be the towns, municipalities and counties across Canada that often have serious concerns about safety. They will not be represented on the committee the Minister proposes to appoint in Bill C-105.
My point is that municipalities, employees and their unions should have far greater representation on this committee. Some people will say that the Minister has the discretionary power to appoint municipal representatives, and so on, to the committee but I feel this is not enough. We should have a system that would guarantee public interest groups are given a number of seats, for instance, Transport 2000, municipalities and so forth, to provide as I said earlier, a balance and ensure that the committee will not only represent a Government that wants to cut costs and railway companies, who also want to cut costs like the Government tells them to, especially in the case of the Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in listening to the Hon. Member's response to the question with regard to whether he believes there should be some sort of job protection for employees of railways who disclose breeches of safety practices, in other words, to use the generic term, whistleblowing protection.
February 5, 1988

I was most interested in his comments in that regard because, as you know, Mr. Speaker, I introduced a private Member's motion on the subject of whistleblowing protection generally within the federal area of competence a few months ago. That particular whistleblowing protection would have included not only the protection of whistleblowers in federally regulated industries and businesses such as railroads, but it would also have protected whistleblowers in Government departments and agencies and those who were engaged in businesses which were contracting with the federal Government. At that time, during the course of the debate-and my motion was talked out, Mr. Speaker-the Hon. Member's Party, the Liberal Party, took a position against that sort of legislation. The spokesman for the Liberal Party spoke out quite strongly against support for whistleblowing legislation.
I wonder if the Hon. Member would have a word with Members of his Party and urge them in future to support this form of whistleblowing legislation, particularly my own motion when 1 bring it forth again in the House?

Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad to respond to the Hon. Member. He, of course, will know that Private Members' motions are just that, Private Members' motions. It is interesting to note-and I invite the Hon. Member to pay attention to this-that most of the people who disagreed with the Hon. Member's motion, although it is true that one Liberal expressed that view, were speaking on behalf of the Conservative Party.
Only one Liberal spoke.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity late this week to make some comments with respect to Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. I must say that over the last number of months I cannot recall how many delegations representing the various railway unions, users of the railways and representatives of CN, CP and VIA Rail, 1 have received. They are all concerned about a variety of issues. I suppose the top of the list would be the low moral we are presently experiencing with our railway employees.
I suspect the number of people in this country who are directly employed by the railways would approach nearly
60,000	and, of course, there are thousands of others who are indirectly employed by either CN, CP or VIA Rail. Therefore, we are talking about a vast number of Canadians and the moral of railway employees is probably at its lowest level ever. One can hardly blame them when one considers that the Government of Canada legislated the workers back to work last August with the promise that the differences between the companies and the employees would be ironed out through an arbitrator. An arbitrator was appointed, but month after month passed, one deadline was reached and extensions were given, and now we are told that the arbitrator is planning
Railway Safety Act
meetings well into April, May and June and, I have heard, as far away as September.
It would appear-and I repeat appear-that the companies have no intention of working to resolve this issue with respect to the working conditions of their employees. It seems that the Government, by giving these extensions to the arbitrator, is almost sympathetic to that view. 1 hope that is not the case.
On the front page of the Globe and Mail yesterday there was a major story with respect to a memo sent by a senior vicepresident of CNR, Mr. Doug Fletcher, indicating to his subordinates that they had better get on with downsizing of each and every aspect of the railway because of the fear that as we get closer and closer to an election, it will become more and more difficult for the railway to do so, for political reasons. I do not know if that memo is accurate. The Globe and Mail published it on its front page, and I suspect it would have ensured that a story of that nature would be well researched. If the railways are downsizing-which is a fancy word for saying laying off people-and from talking to employees across the country one certainly gets that impression, it seems the railways are bent on laying off people.
In Kamloops we have both the CN and CP coming through that community, and have seen the effects of downsizing. We have seen the loss of many, many jobs over the last number of months as the railways rationalize their operations and downsize. While I must admit I have never been a super fan of CN or CP in terms of how they approach their labour relations, I also want to be a little sympathetic because they have been forced to enter into what in many respects could be called an unrealistic competitive world as a result of deregulation in the transportation sector. They are now forced to rationalize their operations, to cut back their operations to the bone in an effort to compete with other modes of transpora-tion, as a result of deregulation.
I realize that this is an ideological debate which I suspect we will have for many years, perhaps forever, with respect to the role our railroads play in terms of competitiveness. If we are trying to do everything as cheaply as possible, that is one route. If we are trying to do things as safely as possible, that is another route. If one is responsible for one of Canada's major railways and sees very clearly that because of the Government's commitment to deregulation one has to cut every corner possible to be competitive with trucking firms from the United States and elsewhere, the one thing that goes by the by, obviously, is safety, safety for employees and safety generally for people living along the rail lines, and for others. That is a fact of life.
Railroaders have consistently heard story after story about the lives of people working on the railways being put at risk. Many people have lost their lives through accidents of one kind or another. There is a growing sense that our railway systems are not becoming safer but in fact more unsafe. The fact that they are moving faster, that they are heavier, and moving more

February 5, 1988
Railway Safety Act
hazardous materials all the time, ought to raise our level of concern as parliamentarians higher than ever.
I also want to say that 1 am happy we are debating this Bill on railway safety. If I recall my history books correctly, CCF Members in the House of Commons in the late 1940s asked for this piece of legislation. I remember all sorts of instances where New Democrats in the House of Commons have called for Liberal and Conservative Governments to bring forward legislation that would enable those people working on or alongside the railways of Canada to do so in a safe environment. We are now debating that kind of legislation and, to be fair, I want to indicate how pleased I am to be doing so.
That pleasure will be reflected in our willingness to expedite this legislation with respect to its debate in the House of Commons and its treatment at whatever committee it might end up. That is not saying we like everything in this piece of legislation. There are things we do not like about it. There are areas where we believe we can suggest improvements through amendments, and we will be doing just that. However, 1 want to make it very clear that we have no intention of doing anything that might hinder the progress of this legislation so that we can see it introduced into reality as soon as possible.,
That becomes very important because I am sure you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, of the vacuum in which we are operating. Because of the deregulation legislation that was introduced into this House not long ago, the CTC and the Rail Transport Committee ceased to exist as of the end of last year. We are now into the next year and are awaiting the National Transportation Agency to set itself up and get its various regulatory organizations in place. That has yet to occur in total. So we are caught in a no-man's land. We are existing in a vacuum when it comes to railway safety. So 1 think it is in the interest of all of us to ensure we progress expeditiously and do what we can not only to improve this legislation but to see it passed in amended form.
Perhaps it would be useful to look at some of the statistics over the last little while in terms of what has been going on with our rail systems across Canada. You would be interested, Mr. Speaker, to learn that since 1982 we have experienced 1,318 train derailments. From my recollection, it would seem that most of those occurred in my constituency which is in the mountainous area of British Columbia where both the CN and CP travel through some incredibly scenic country. That is another way of saying very mountainous and rough terrain. It is a wonder that we do not have more derailments. There have been 1,318 train derailments that have resulted in a few fatalities, fortunately not too many.
Let us now look at collisions, which is another category when we talk about rail safety. Since 1982 there have been nearly 450 train collisions. Of course, part of this is because of those over-zealous dispatchers who, in the effort to move material more rapidly across the country to generate more
transportation business, often have more than one train in the same section of the track at the same time. This has resulted in some problems which have resulted, inevitably, in a collision with a number of fatalities I am sorry to have to say.
The main area of concern in terms of fatalities is associated with crossing accidents. I refer to level crossings where one is required to cross a train track, whether one is travelling in a car, a truck or some other kind of vehicle. We have had 3,437 crossing accidents since 1982 resulting in 361 fatalities, to say nothing of the very serious injuries which have occurred because of these accidents.
When we look at the last six years, we find that hundreds and hundreds of deaths have occurred as a result of crossing accidents, train collisions or derailments. Obviously, when we consider legislation dealing with rail safety its importance becomes very evident indeed.
One of the aspects that perplexes me about this legislation, and I recognize that we are not talking about the specifics of it but about the principles involved in it, is that it does not set very high standards at all. As a matter of fact, in most areas it does not set any standards. We are told that that will come at a later time when the Government introduces regulations. For example, there is nothing in the Bill that provides specifics with respect to the frequency of inspections. When will these regular inspections occur, weekly, monthly, yearly, biannually, when?
The Government has decided to take the cabooses off our trains. Many people who make their living on those same trains say that this will result in less safety. They say that the removal of the cabooses will result in more train mishaps. As a result the whole matter of inspection frequency becomes a major item of concern. When cabooses are not on these trains there will be instead what is called special boxes and the like to do the monitoring. There will be people to do some visual monitoring as well. We are talking about some very sophisticated, heavy equipment. As a result inspection frequency becomes a critical issue, to say nothing of the specifics regarding the maintenance of track and equipment. If we are talking about a Bill regarding rail safety, it is not unrealistic to expect that it will have to say something about the maintenance of equipment and tracks which criss-cross the country. However, the Bill is mute when it comes to these areas. As I have said, regulations will come later.
While some people would suggest that unfairness has become a hallmark of the Government, when we consider this piece of legislation we see that there are some unfair aspects to it as well. I refer specifically to the area concerning penalties and the regulations which will be developed. There are expectations in the Bill for companies as well as individuals. If one breaks the regulations or fails to comply with them then there will be penalties to be paid. This legislation virtually does not distinguish between individuals and corporations such as the CPR. If one is found to be guilty of having committed an infraction and one is an individual, then one could receive a
February 5, 1988

fine of up to $10,000, and spend time in jail. However, if one is the CPR and is found to be in contravention of some aspect of this legislation, then one could actually receive a fine of up to $50,000.
CPR is one of the largest corporations in the western world. It has assets in the billions and billions of dollars, with revenues in the many billions of dollars. To think that it could actually be fined up to $50,000 is hardly what one would think is something that will deter the CPR, the CNR or VIA Rail. The point I am trying to make is that this provision is probably a licence fee to be unsafe, since if one is caught and is found guilty one would receive a fine of a few thousand dollars. That will not do anything to encourage the CPR, the CNR or VIA Rail to change some of their habits.
In terms of the theme of unfairness I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the railway safety consultative committee which is the committee that will be set up under this legislation to advise on a whole variety of areas. Let us consider the make-up of this committee. The Minister himself or herself will be able to appoint five members to the committee. The railway companies will be able to appoint five members to the committee. The employees, who represent 60,000 individuals, will have but one member on the committee. I think it is initiatives such as this that send a very clear message to the rank and file employees of our railways that their concerns and their views are irrelevant. Quite frankly, there should be 10 employee representatives on the committee, in addition to the five appointed by the Minister and the five appointed by the companies. This would send a clear signal that the views of the employees are respected and that their welfare is utmost in the mind of the Government. I can only interpret this provision to mean that that, unfortunately, is not the case.
There is another area in the legislation which is also of great concern to me. It has to do with the protection for employees who recognize that what they have to do or what they are being requested to do by their superior is unsafe. What course of events may employees such as these pursue? What course of action is open to them when they find themselves in such a situation? The Bill has no provisions for this type of situation. It simply indicates that the employee should report to his or her superior and complain about his or her decision. You can imagine a situation, Mr. Speaker, when someone's boss tells him or her to do a certain thing, that is, to ride a train in a certain way or to deal with a piece of equipment that that person knows to be unsafe because he or she works in that environment every day, and he or she refuses to do it. That person will be in deep trouble. Obviously, if he or she goes against the wishes of the superior then that person will be harassed. He or she can expect some type of disciplinary action. There is no protection in the Bill for the employee.
If we are going to run the type of incredibly vast railway system that we have in Canada then we must want to have the employees on side. I am always amazed at the tremendous amount of loyalty that actually exists in the train community, if I can use that term, where employees of CPR, CNR and
Railway Safety Act
VIA are committed to their work and the companies in terms of serving them in spite of the harassment and in spite of the incredible conditions under which they are forced to work.
I referred earlier to a copy of a memo that was printed in The Globe and Mail of yesterday in which the Vice-President of the CNR states that the company must move expeditiously to lay off as many people as it can as quickly as it can so that it does not become a political issue in the next federal election campaign. That is not the way to build morale with one's employees.
I want to conclude my remarks by referring to an article by Professor Brian Tucker who teaches organizational behaviour at the University of Saskatchewan's College of Commerce. For some time now he has spent much of his effort and expertise examining the whole matter of stress experienced by railway employees. He has interviewed individuals who work for the railway. Of course, much of our attention was focused on the terrible incident near Hinton, Alberta, that killed 23 people in February, 1986.
That incident prompted Professor Tucker to do some analysis of what it is that causes problems on our rail systems. He figured that stress was a major factor. In this era of deregulation when competition requires companies to cut corners at every opportunity, often the employees are pushed to limits that are simply unacceptable in terms of normal human behaviour. The other day 1 heard representations from railway employees who live in Kamloops. They indicated the type of shifts that they were expected to work, the hours and hours that they were expected to be alert and on the job and finely tuned in terms of safety conditions. After a person works for many hours in one day, has a short sleep, and is back again for another long shift, the level of stress and the alertness and ability becomes problematic.
Brian Tucker spent much time looking at the railroad system. In the article he states:
In the macho culture of the railways, stress is a taboo topic. Trainmen are
not supposed to be affected by work-related or domestic stress. If they can't
stand the heat, they're supposed to get out of the locomotive.
That is an interesting observation and an interesting code, but the reality is that those people do have work related stress, and they do have domestic related stress. Quite frankly, what is needed is a change in the culture and the working environment on the railways to reduce this stress. When employees of the railroads of Canada read in yesterday's Globe and Mail that one of the senior vice-presidents of CPR is encouraging maximum lay-offs to occur immediately, that is not the type of comment that builds confidence and generates positive morale in a corporation.
In co-operation with the federal Government, because we are dealing with federal legislation and CN is a Crown corporation, and we know the ownership pattern of VIA, it is in the best interest of the rail companies and the federal

February 5, 1988
Environmental Affairs
Government to work co-operatively to build a sense of positive morale with the employees across Canada, the 60,000 men and women who make our railways run. If they all had a feeling that their jobs were secure, their futures were secure, and that their contribution is recognized, the productivity would inevitably increase substantially.
If one reads any book on management the theme is that an employee who feels confident, secure, understood, and recognized will perform at the highest level possible. Unfortunately, those conditions do not exist within the railways of Canada today. I am afraid to say it, but much of the legislation of the federal Government has abetted the downward spiralling of morale.
In conclusion, this legislation is welcome. I appreciate the fact that we are debating the Railway Safety Act. Our intention is to co-operate as much as possible not only to ensure that the Bill moves quickly, but that the final legislation that is passed at third reading is the very best possible.

Mr. Speaker, there are two things that I would like my colleague to comment on. One is the situation in his own community of Kamloops, and what he can tell us about any lay-offs there. A couple of years ago I was told about one railroad that reduced its number of carmen from nine to four. Those are the people who do the inspections and the minor repairs.
The other thing I would like to ask him is if he can comment on what he thinks would be appropriate penalties for railways, and should it also include railway officers.
You may not be aware, Mr. Speaker, but the only way to find out how much the officers of Canadian Pacific or Canadian National get paid is to go to the U.S. Securities Exchange Commission in Washington. That information cannot be found out in Canada, but the United States law requires that information. The last time I saw any figures, the President of Canadian Pacific Ltd. receives about 12 or 13 times as much as the highest paid locomotive engineer. The last time I received a figure it was $656,000 a year that that President received. I have often wondered if perhaps an appropriate penalty would not be a fine on the President of Canadian Pacific Ltd. of 13 times as much as an ordinary employee would be fined, and perhaps also a jail term for that President who is also an employee.
Would the Hon. Member comment on what he thinks would be an appropriate fine? Should it be on officers of the company as well as the company itself?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Regina West jogged my memory, and I want to make one other comment today as we are debating railway safety. Of course, railway safety to a large extent is a reflection of the willingness of employees and others to co-operate with regulations and so on. As those people wait for their contract after the Government of Canada legislated them back to work, what was interesting is that the management received their raises for the year. They
received a substantial raise prior to the employees receiving theirs. Those of us here who in the past, or even at the present, have had employees, know that that is not a rule that one normally follows. Once the contract is settled with the employees, then one is in a position to consider the increases to the management personnel. The railways do it the opposite way around which again aggravates a serious situation.
With respect to the two questions from my hon. friend from Regina West. The situation in Kamloops is that, yes, there have been lay-offs over the last number of months; and, yes, they were in the inspection and repair areas. In a hard pressed part of Canada, the central part of British Columbia, where the unemployment rates in some communities are running as high as 40 per cent, this was a very serious blow. However, all of this happens in the spirit of deregulation and the fact that the federal Government is forcing cut-backs on the railway companies.
Returning to the suggestion of my hon. colleague that we ought to reconsider the penalties. When an individual can be fined up to $10,000 or receive a term in jail for an infraction and the company management do not exist under those same conditions, it is only fair, if we are going to have that type of penalty, that officers of the company be eligible for the same treatment. It is obviously ridiculous to consider a maximum fine of $50,000 for a company like CPR. The fine should probably be 10 times that figure, or perhaps something to approximate the annual salary of the President of CPR which is in the $600,000 range plus bonuses. Perhaps that would be an appropriate criteria to use.
To be serious, Mr. Speaker, certainly all I can say as a lay person in the area of railways, $50,000 as a fine for a company like CPR or CNR is obviously ridiculous.
